85.title: The hare in the moon
85.hook: a hare with nothing to give offers himself to a hungry guest; his image is set on the moon (Jataka 316)
85.howItsDone: Jataka tales like the hare's are told to children, painted on temple walls and performed as plays across Buddhist Asia, and Buddhists hear in them the perfections, such as generosity, that the Buddha is said to have practiced over many lives.

segments.voice: Yesterday: parinibbana, and the last words: all things put together come apart, so keep going. Your line: strive on with care. A new week starts today: the Jataka, as shorts.

Tonight, if the sky is clear, look up at the moon. Some people see a face there. In stories told from India to Japan, people see a hare. Now the path turns to something lighter and very old: the Jataka tales, a great collection of stories that tradition says the Buddha told about his own earlier lives, as an animal, a king, a merchant, a monkey. They were painted on temple walls and carved on stone gates, and they're still told to children. The first one this week begins in a forest, with four friends: an otter, a jackal, a monkey, and a hare.
screen: `A HARE IN THE MOON.` → `THE JATAKA: EARLIER LIVES.` → `FOUR FRIENDS IN A FOREST.`

segments.voice: The hare is wise, and he teaches the others. One day he says: tomorrow is a holy day. Let's keep it well, and if anyone comes asking for food, let's give from what we have. Next morning, each goes out. The otter finds fish on a riverbank. The jackal finds some meat and a pot of curds. The monkey brings mangoes. But the hare only eats grass. I can't offer anyone grass, he thinks. If a hungry guest comes, I'll give him my own body. Sakka, the king of the gods, hears of this and decides to test it. Disguised as a hungry traveler, he visits each friend in turn. The otter offers fish, the jackal meat, the monkey mangoes. Then he comes to the hare, who says: gather some wood and make a fire. I'll give you something I've never given before. The fire is lit. The hare shakes himself three times, so any tiny creatures in his fur can escape unharmed. And he leaps into the flames. But the fire is cold. Not a hair on him is singed. The traveler reveals himself as Sakka, come only to test him. So that the hare's gift will be remembered, he draws the hare's image on the face of the moon, to last through this whole age of the world. Whatever anyone sees in the moon, the story's shape is plain. The hare had the least of anyone, and gave the most, the one thing he had. And even then, he shook himself first.

segments.voice: Some days there doesn't seem to be much to give, not much money, not much energy. Ask yourself, like the hare: what do I actually have? Time, attention, a skill, a listening ear, a good laugh. Pick one, and picture giving it, fully, to someone who needs it.
Sasa. The hare who, with only grass to give, offered his whole self to a hungry guest, and whose image was drawn on the moon.
Your line: give what you have. Grass was all he had, so he offered himself. See you tomorrow.

86.title: The banyan deer
86.hook: a deer king takes the place of a pregnant doe; the hunting king is moved to stop the hunt (Jataka 12)
86.howItsDone: The banyan deer story is told in Buddhist schools and temples to illustrate compassion and self-sacrifice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sasa, the hare who had only grass and gave himself. Your line: give what you have.

Have you ever taken someone's shift so they could be at a birth, or a funeral, or just sleep? Somebody's turn was coming, and you stepped in. In the days when Brahmadatta ruled Benares, the story goes, the king loved to hunt deer, and every day he dragged the townspeople out of their fields to help. Tired of it, the people drove a whole forest of deer into the king's park, shut the gate, and said: there. Hunt them there. In that park were two herds, each with its own king. One was a golden deer called Banyan, our hero. The other was called Branch.
screen: `TAKING SOMEONE'S SHIFT.` → `A KING WHO LOVED TO HUNT.` → `TWO HERDS IN ONE PARK.`

segments.voice: Every day the king or his cook came and shot at the deer, and many were wounded in the chaos, not just the one taken. So Banyan went to Branch with a grim deal: let's draw lots. One deer each day goes to the chopping block on its own, and the herds take turns. Fewer will suffer. The king, who admired the two golden deer, had already promised never to kill their leaders. One day the lot falls on a doe in Branch's herd who is about to give birth. Let me have my fawn first, she asks her king, and then I'll go. Branch refuses: it's your turn. Go. So she goes to Banyan. And Banyan says: go home. I'll take your turn. He walks to the block and lays his head on it. The cook runs to tell the king, who comes and says: I spared you. Why are you here? The deer explains about the doe, and the king is moved beyond words. I have never seen such kindness, even among people, he says. Get up. I spare your life and hers. And the rest of the deer? Banyan asks. Them too. And the other animals in the forest? Them too. And the birds? The fish in the water? One by one, the deer king asks, until every creature has been given its safety. Tradition says this was one of the Buddha's earlier lives. The Jataka's closing verse boils down to this: better to stay close to Banyan than to live with Branch.

segments.voice: Think of who around you is carrying something heavy right now: a new parent, a worn-out coworker, a friend with a sick relative. Picture one of them, and yourself stepping in for one small thing, the dishes, the school run, a phone call they dread. You don't have to lay your head on a block; one turn is enough.

87.title: The talkative tortoise
87.hook: two geese carry a tortoise on a stick; he opens his mouth to answer the jeers and falls (Jataka 215)
87.howItsDone: The talkative tortoise is told to children in Buddhist homes and schools, and Buddhist teaching counts right speech, including knowing when not to speak, as part of the eightfold path.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nigrodha, the banyan deer, who laid his head on the block in a mother's place. Your line: stand in for someone.

A comeback, typed and ready. A thumb hovering over send. Someone in the comments said something smug, and the reply is right there. Hold that moment. There was once a king of Benares, the story goes, who talked too much. Nobody else could get a word in. His wise adviser, who tradition says was the Buddha in an earlier life, had been waiting for a way to tell him so without getting in trouble. Then one day a tortoise fell out of the sky and landed in the palace courtyard, split in two. The king asked how on earth that happened, and the adviser told him.
screen: `THE PERFECT COMEBACK.` → `A KING WHO TALKED TOO MUCH.` → `A TORTOISE FALLS FROM THE SKY.`

segments.voice: Up in the mountains, a tortoise lived in a lake, and two young wild geese used to come there to feed. They became friends. Come home with us, the geese said. We live in a golden cave in the Himalayas. It's beautiful. How? said the tortoise. I can't fly. The geese had an idea: we'll hold the two ends of a stick in our beaks, you bite down on the middle, and we'll fly you there. Just one thing. Keep your mouth shut the whole way. Not a word. Off they go, a goose at each end, the tortoise clamped on the middle. Over a village, the children look up and shout: look, look! Two geese carrying a tortoise on a stick! The tortoise gets angry. He wants to say: if my friends want to carry me, what's it to you, you brats? He opens his mouth to say it, lets go of the stick, and down he falls, right into the king's courtyard. The adviser turns to the king and says, gently: this is what happens to people who can't hold their tongue. The Jataka says the king understood the story was about him, and from then on he spoke less. The good thing here: the tortoise isn't wicked. He isn't even wrong; the kids really were being rude. He just couldn't let it go unanswered, and that one reply cost him everything. The same story is told in other Indian fable collections too, like the Panchatantra. The tortoise could be anyone with a thumb over send.

segments.voice: Remember a moment when someone said something that stung and you wanted to fire back, and feel the words line up, ready to go. Now, like the tortoise on the stick, keep your mouth closed and breathe through your nose, letting the words stay unspoken. Notice that you're still flying.

88.title: The quarrelling quails
88.hook: the quails lift the net together and fly off, until they start to bicker (Jataka 33)
88.howItsDone: The quail story is told in Buddhist communities as a lesson in harmony, and harmony in the sangha, the monastic community, is something Buddhist monastic rules work hard to protect.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kacchapa, the tortoise who opened his mouth to answer the jeers, and fell. Your line: not every word needs saying.

Any group that's pulled off something hard together, a band, a team, a family moving house, knows the moment it starts to go wrong. It's rarely the big challenge that breaks it. It's the small stuff. Who left the dishes. Who didn't pull their weight. This Jataka is set in a forest where many thousands of quails live under one wise leader, and the leader, in this telling, is the Buddha-to-be. A bird-catcher lived nearby. He'd imitate the quail call, throw his net over them when they gathered, and carry them off to sell. So the wise quail made a plan.
screen: `IT'S RARELY THE BIG CHALLENGE.` → `THOUSANDS OF QUAILS, ONE LEADER.` → `A BIRD-CATCHER'S NET.`

segments.voice: When the net falls on us, the leader says, every one of you put your head through a hole in the mesh. Then all together, lift, and fly. Carry the net to a thorn bush, drop it there, and slip out from underneath. It works. The next time the bird-catcher throws his net, thousands of little heads pop up through the mesh, and the whole net rises like a sail and floats off to a thorn bush. He spends the evening untangling it from the thorns, empty-handed. Day after day. His wife starts asking questions. Then one day, as the quails are landing to feed, one accidentally steps on another's head. Who stepped on my head? I did, sorry, I didn't mean it. But the other one won't let it go, and the argument grows. Oh, I suppose you think you're the one lifting the whole net by yourself? The wise quail sees it and knows: when quarreling starts, disaster isn't far behind. He leads the quails who'll follow him away to another place. The bird-catcher bides his time. A few days later he throws his net again, over the ones who stayed, and they're still bickering. You lift it. No, you lift it. I lifted it last time, your turn. While they argue about who should lift, nobody lifts at all, and he gathers the net and carries them all away. The enemy isn't what beats them. The net was always there. It only closed when they stopped lifting together.

segments.voice: Think of a group you belong to, a family, a team, a household, and any small squabble going on: who does what, whose turn it is. Picture everyone under the same net. Now picture yourself, instead of arguing about who should lift, just lifting your end, with no score kept.
Sammodamana. Living in harmony: the quails who together lifted the bird-catcher's net and flew free, until they started bickering about who was lifting.
Your line: together we lift the net. Thousands of little heads, one rising sail. Eighty-eight days now.

89.title: The monkey and the crocodile
89.hook: caught mid-river, the monkey says he left his heart up in the fig tree (Jataka 208)
89.howItsDone: The monkey and the crocodile is told to children in Buddhist homes and schools, appears in early Buddhist carving, and is found in the Panchatantra as well.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sammodamana, the quails who lifted the net together until they started bickering. Your line: together we lift the net.

Sometimes the trouble only shows itself halfway across. The friendly stranger isn't friendly. The deal isn't a deal. And the only way out is quick thinking. On the bank of the Ganges, the story goes, there lived a monkey, strong and clever. Tradition says it was the Buddha, in an earlier life. In the river lived a crocodile, whose wife had been watching the monkey leap through the trees. One day she said to her husband: I have a craving. I want to eat that monkey's heart.
screen: `HALFWAY ACROSS.` → `A MONKEY ON THE GANGES.` → `I WANT THAT MONKEY'S HEART.`

segments.voice: The crocodile swims up to the bank, all friendliness. Why stay on this side, eating the same old fruit? Across the river there are mango trees, jackfruit, the sweetest fruit you've ever tasted. Climb on my back, and I'll take you. That sounds wonderful, and the monkey hops on. Out in the middle of the river, the crocodile starts to sink. Water up to the monkey's knees. His chest. Hey, what are you doing? And the crocodile, sure he's won, tells the truth. My wife wants your heart. I'm going to drown you and bring it to her. The monkey can't fight. He can't swim to shore. So he laughs. Oh, friend, you should have said so! We monkeys don't keep our hearts inside us when we're out and about. We'd smash them to pieces, jumping from branch to branch. We hang them up in a tree for safekeeping. See that fig tree, with all the round fruit hanging on it? Those are our hearts. Take me back and I'll give you mine. The crocodile, not the brightest, swims back to the bank. The monkey leaps off, up into the fig tree, and calls down: you big fool. Did you really think anyone keeps his heart in a treetop? You're huge, but you have no wits at all. What makes this one lovely is where the monkey's strength came from. Not muscles. Not claws. A calm mind, in deep water, that saw a way out force could never find.

90.title: The golden goose
90.hook: a golden bird gives one feather at a time; the greedy wife plucks it bare and the gold turns ordinary (Jataka 136)
90.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the golden goose story to teach contentment (santutthi), and the Jataka's frame story ties it to a monastic rule about taking more than was offered.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sumsumara, the crocodile, and a monkey who said his heart was in the fig tree. Your line: keep your wits.

You've probably heard of the goose that laid golden eggs: the farmer cut it open to get all the gold at once, and got nothing. That's Aesop. The Jataka has a cousin of it, stranger and sadder. A good man dies and leaves a wife and three daughters with almost nothing. He's reborn, tradition says, as a goose with feathers of pure gold, and one day he remembers his old life and the family he left. He flies to find them, living poor, working for other people, and lands on their roof.
screen: `NOT THE GOOSE WITH THE EGGS.` → `A FATHER REBORN AS A GOLDEN GOOSE.` → `HE FLIES HOME.`

segments.voice: The family is frightened at first. Then the goose tells them who he is. I was your husband, your father. I've come to help. Each time I come, I'll leave you one of my golden feathers. And he does. They sell the feathers, and little by little life gets easier: food, a little comfort. Then the mother starts thinking. Birds can't be trusted, she tells her daughters. One day he'll just stop coming. Next time, let's pluck him bare and get all the gold at once. The daughters refuse: that would hurt him. But the next time the goose comes, the mother grabs him and pulls out every feather. And the gold turns ordinary: plain feathers, no better than a crane's. The story says only that they were plucked against his will; some readers take the point to be that the gold was his to give, and taken by force, it was gold no more. His wings are bare. He can't fly. They put him in a big jar and feed him, and in time his feathers grow back, plain white. When he can fly again, he flies away, and never comes back. The verse at the end of the Jataka says something like: be content with what you're given; greed loses even the gold you had. Notice the shape of it. No punishment from outside. The gift simply couldn't survive being grabbed. One feather at a time, freely given, was more than enough.

segments.voice: Something good in your life may come a little at a time: a friendship, rest, a person's patience, money, maybe. Notice any part of you that wants to grab it all, now, just in case, and feel the grip. Then, on an out-breath, loosen it; one feather at a time is enough.
Hamsa. The golden goose: a father reborn as this bird, giving one feather at a time, until greed plucked him bare and the gold turned ordinary.
Your line: greed plucks the goose bare. The daughters said no; the mother grabbed. Ninety days, just like that.

91.title: The ruru deer
91.hook: a golden deer saves a drowning man, who later betrays him to the king
91.howItsDone: Buddhists tell Jataka stories like this one in temples, schools and at home, and Buddhist teaching holds up doing good without expecting a return as part of the perfection of giving.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hamsa, the golden goose, one feather at a time, until greed pulled them all and the gold turned plain. Your line: greed plucks the goose bare.

Money lent and quietly never mentioned again. A favor nobody returned. A door held open, and the person walks through looking at a phone. A small voice says: next time, don't bother. Today's story is for that voice, and it's the last of the short stories: number 482 in the Jataka, the tales of the Buddha's earlier lives. A deer with a coat like gold, a river in flood, and a man shouting for help. A short story about a long question: why do good for people who won't thank you?
screen: `A FAVOR NOBODY RETURNED.` → `NEXT TIME, DON'T BOTHER?` → `A RIVER IN FLOOD.`

segments.voice: A young man from a rich family has wasted everything. Buried in debt, he throws himself into the Ganges. Then, in the water, he changes his mind and screams for help. On the bank lives a ruru deer, the Bodhisatta, the Buddha-to-be, with golden skin and a gentle voice. He wades into the current, lets the man grab hold, and carries him to shore. He warms him, feeds him, shows him the road home, and asks one thing: don't tell anyone where I live. The man promises. Meanwhile, in the city, the queen dreams of a golden deer teaching the law, and asks the king to find him. The king offers a reward: a village, and a thousand coins. The man he saved hears it, goes straight to the palace, and leads the king to the river. The king raises his bow. The deer speaks, in a human voice, and asks who showed him the way. Hearing the whole story, the king is so disgusted he wants to shoot the traitor instead. And here's the turn that makes it a Jataka. The deer steps between them and asks the king to spare the man. He's still saving him. The king lets him go, takes the deer to the city with honor, and the deer teaches the court. The point isn't that people are awful, though the story is honest that some are. It's where the deer's goodness lives. It never depended on the man's gratitude. The ingratitude doesn't cancel the rescue. It just shows who each of them was.
screen: `A MAN IN THE FLOOD.` · `THE DEER CARRIES HIM OUT.` · `THE MAN SELLS HIM TO THE KING.` · `THE DEER SAVES HIM AGAIN.` · then, large: `DO IT ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one good thing you did that nobody thanked you for, and notice whatever comes with it, maybe a sting, maybe a little scorekeeping. Now picture the deer on the riverbank, choosing to wade in, and let your act stand on its own, finished and complete, whether or not anyone saw. If a thought comes up about what they owe you, let it float past like a leaf on the river.
Ruru. The golden deer who saved a drowning man, was betrayed by him, and then saved him again.
Your line: do it anyway. The deer saved him twice, and never asked for thanks. See you tomorrow.
